$comment: GOLDEN CONTRACT FIXTURE — HITL ticket v1 (issue #4178).
The ask an agent makes when it needs a human decision, and the answer that
comes back. `models.py` in this directory is the normative validator;
against it on every PR that touches either. A golden fixture prevents
Consumers: NONE YET. This contract deliberately lands before the
implementations that adopt it, so the two divergent approval paths
`while (true)`) can be reconciled against a written shape instead of
against each other. When a consumer arrives, add it to this list and to the
workflow's paths filter — that is what keeps the fixture load-bearing.
The rejected_variants below are not hypotheticals. Each one is a shape that
would compile, read plausibly in review, and silently weaken the fail-closed
guarantee. They are the reason this file exists rather than prose alone.

accepted_ticket.$comment: A destructive-action ask with named approvers — the tightest configuration the contract supports, and the one a multi-day agent hits when it wants to force-push or destroy infrastructure.
accepted_ticket.name: hitl-ticket
accepted_ticket.prompt: Agent run 55155b28 wants to run `terraform destroy` against the dev VPC module (14 resources, including the RDS instance). Approve this one action?

accepted_ticket_gate_stage.$comment: The AIDLC gate expressed as a ticket — proves the contract can describe the mechanism ADP already runs, rather than a fiction. `approvers.mode: any-maintainer` with no identities is valid; identities is only required under mode 'named'. `context` is omitted entirely to prove it is optional.

Paired with the `rejected` response above, this is the distinction the whole four-value vocabulary exists for: same ticket, same non-permissive outcome, materially different cause. A retry is reasonable here and wrong above. `answered_by` is a system component, not a human.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: permissive_on_expiry
rejected_ticket_variants.why: A timeout that APPROVES. This is the single worst shape the contract can permit: an agent asks for permission to do something destructive, nobody answers, and silence becomes consent. Invariant 3 forbids it, so `allowed-once` in on_expiry must fail validation, not merely be discouraged in prose.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: approvers_absent
rejected_ticket_variants.why: No authorization predicate at all. This is the shape ADP's two live implementations effectively have — any commenter's '/approve' counts — and it is why an unauthorized party can satisfy an approval today. `approvers` is required so a consumer always has something to check identity against.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: named_mode_empty_identities
rejected_ticket_variants.why: mode='named' with nobody named. Approvable by no one, but it does not look broken — it would sit until timeout and read as human indifference rather than a malformed ask. Rejecting it makes an unanswerable-but-approvable ticket unconstructable.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: expiry_result_not_in_options
rejected_ticket_variants.why: on_expiry names a human choice the ticket never offered, so the answer synthesized at timeout is not a valid answer to this ticket. Non-permissive and therefore safe, but incoherent — a consumer validating the synthesized response against options would reject its own timeout. Note the exemption: the SYSTEM results ('cancelled', 'unavailable') are always valid answers and need no entry in options, so this variant uses 'rejected', which IS a human choice.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: options_empty
rejected_ticket_variants.why: A ticket that permits no answers. Unanswerable by construction.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: unknown_scope
rejected_ticket_variants.why: The scope vocabulary is closed so consumers can route and audit by scope without matching on free text. An unrecognized scope would fall through every routing branch.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: naive_expires_at
rejected_ticket_variants.why: A timezone-naive deadline means 'whatever the reader's clock says'. A durable ticket outlives the process that wrote it, so the reader is a different machine than the writer — the ambiguity is guaranteed to bite, not merely possible.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: ticket_id_empty
rejected_ticket_variants.why: An empty ticket_id defeats the named-intent rule as surely as a missing one: every response would bind to the same empty target.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: wrong_version
rejected_ticket_variants.why: A v2 document must not validate as v1. Consumers pin to a version (contracts/README.md versioning rules); silently accepting a different one is how a pinned consumer ends up parsing a shape it does not understand.

rejected_ticket_variants.name: unknown_field
rejected_ticket_variants.why: extra='forbid'. An unrecognized key is either a typo in a field that matters or a consumer inventing unversioned semantics; both must surface at the boundary. `context` is the one place extras are allowed, on purpose.

rejected_response_variants.name: response_missing_ticket_id
rejected_response_variants.why: THE named-vs-positional rule (invariant 2). Without a ticket_id, a response is positional: it answers 'the pending request', and if two are pending, a human approving X can authorize Y. This is the variant that must never regress.

rejected_response_variants.name: response_allowed_always
rejected_response_variants.why: v1 has no durable-grant escape hatch. A persistent grant is a policy decision with its own audit and revocation story, not an answer to a question. If 'allowed-always' validated, the first adopter would use it and the non-durable guarantee would be gone before anyone noticed.

rejected_response_variants.name: response_unknown_result
rejected_response_variants.why: The vocabulary is closed so a typo cannot become a silent permit. An open enum plus a consumer written as `if (result !== 'rejected') proceed()` turns 'aproved' into an approval.

rejected_response_variants.name: response_result_true
rejected_response_variants.why: The boolean shape both live implementations use today ({approved: true}). A two-valued result cannot express 'nobody could be asked', which is precisely the collapse this contract undoes; it must not validate.

rejected_response_variants.name: response_missing_answered_by
rejected_response_variants.why: Identity is required for EVERY result, not just approvals. Without it, invariant 4 is uncheckable — a consumer cannot ask whether the answering principal was permitted to answer.

rejected_response_variants.name: response_empty_answered_by
rejected_response_variants.why: An empty identity is an unverifiable one; it satisfies 'the field is present' while carrying nothing to check against approvers.

rejected_response_variants.name: response_naive_answered_at
rejected_response_variants.why: Same clock ambiguity as expires_at, and the comparison between the two decides whether an answer arrived before the deadline.

rejected_response_variants.name: response_missing_result
rejected_response_variants.why: An answer with no result. Absence must be a validation error rather than defaulting — a default here would be either an accidental permit or a silent denial, and neither should be implicit.
